newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill given finishing touches ahead of vote.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill given finishing touches ahead of vote.

text.p: Tax writers dropped education and Amtrak proposals Wednesday to overcome last-minute haggling over details and a threatened presidential veto ahead of the vote in Congress.
The final tally put the five-year package at a $95 billion net tax cut, bigger than the $85 billion agreed to by the White House and congressional leaders in the May budget pact.
The House and Senate were expected to vote on the tax bill Thursday. The House passed a companion spending bill Wednesday and the Senate was to vote on it Thursday morning.
An education tax break provision aimed at parents with children in elementary and high schools was eliminated after President Clinton threatened to veto the bill over it.

The legislation was held up early Wednesday as Republicans and the White House tried to reach a compromise that would allow the Amtrak railroad to access $2.3 billion in tax credits included in the bill.

Senate Republicans offered to include a Caribbean trade provision in the legislation that the White House was seeking in exchange for acceptance of the Republican Amtrak reform package. But the White House would not agree to that.
A comprehensive package of labour and other reforms must be enacted before the national rail system can access the tax credits.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer said there was a late flurry of pressure to include last-minute items in the tax bill which he resisted. "There has been pressure to do exactly that," the Texas Republican said.

"That's not to say that there have not been some unusual provisions that may have been forced into the bill earlier. The Amtrak provision was a rather unusual provision in the way that it was designed," he added.
The Caribbean Basin Initiative (CBI) sought by the White House would give those countries trade provisions similar to countries in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
NAFTA reduced tariffs on imports from Mexico to levels below those on goods from the Caribbean and countries in that region say they have lost apparel trade to Mexico.

On Amtrak, Republicans had made four proposals, the most controversial of which would require the railroad to negotiate under prevailing labour laws the severance pay and benefits with laid-off workers and allow Amtrak to contract out work. Currently if Amtrak closes a route it is obligated to pay six years severance. Labour unions opposed the Republican plan.
Meanwhile, Republican legislators released a letter from Clinton to House Speaker Newt Gingrich that was delivered Tuesday night on the education provision that was dropped.

At issue was a proposal by Sen. Paul Coverdell, a Georgia Republican, which would have allowed parents to contribute $2,000 a year after tax to an education account, similar to an Individual Retirement Account. The interest earned on that money would be tax-free if used for the child's education.

"As you know, in working out the final agreement, I strongly opposed the Coverdell amendment," Clinton wrote in the letter dated Tuesday. "I would veto any tax package that would undermine public education by providing tax benefits for private and parochial school expenses," the letter said.
Coverdell said after the letter threatening a veto was delivered, his proposal was dropped from the bill. "I don't believe any of us would have the whole (tax bill) go down with it," Coverdell said.
